A hardware privacy display uses special display layers that physically narrow the viewing angle. It needs display hardware support.\n\nSoftware privacy, like this app, uses overlays, masking and optional face detection. It makes the screen harder to read from the side, but it cannot change how your display emits light.

Privacy Display stores only its own settings, on this device. It never uploads camera frames, never saves face images or videos, and never reads your contacts, messages, passwords or screen contents. Face recognition only runs if you turn on owner protection: your face print (numbers, not a photo) is then stored encrypted on this phone and you can delete it at any time.

A phone screen shows the same picture in every direction, so an app cannot make it look blurry only to people at an angle. Instead, the front camera watches for other faces to your left, right, above or below, and blurs the whole screen while they are looking. Nothing is recorded.

The front camera checks whether the person using the phone is you. If not, the screen goes black and taps are blocked until you unlock with your fingerprint or PIN.
It is a deterrent, not a replacement for your lock screen: a photo of you could fool it, it may not recognise you in the dark, and it cannot stop someone from opening Android Settings. It also uses the camera whenever the screen is on, which uses more battery.
